title: Embolization of the Middle Meningeal Artery for Chronic Subdural Hematoma
summary: STEM randomized 310 patients with symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma to adjunctive middle meningeal artery embolization or standard treatment alone after surgical or nonsurgical standard treatment had been selected. In the primary efficacy analysis, the 180-day composite treatment-failure endpoint occurred in 16% with embolization versus 36% with control (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.20-0.66; P=0.001). Major disabling stroke or death within 30 days occurred in 3% in each group.
findings: The primary efficacy composite occurred in 16% with embolization versus 36% with control (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.20-0.66; P=0.001).
Major disabling stroke or death within 30 days occurred in 3% in each group.
Through 180 days, mortality was 8% with embolization versus 5% with control; neurologic death was 1% versus 2%.
Of 310 enrolled participants, 189 had surgical and 121 nonsurgical standard treatment selected before randomization.
comparator: Preselected standard surgical or nonsurgical treatment alone.
population: Adults with symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma for whom surgical or nonsurgical standard treatment had been selected before randomization.
shortTitle: STEM: adjunctive MMA embolization for chronic subdural hematoma
limitations: The efficacy endpoint was a composite mixing residual hematoma, reintervention, and major clinical events, and the primary efficacy analysis included fewer patients than the 310 enrolled. Mortality through 180 days was numerically 8% versus 5%, and the trial was funded by Balt USA; other concurrent trials, particularly MAGIC-MT, did not meet their primary efficacy endpoint.
intervention: Middle meningeal artery embolization as an adjunct to preselected standard surgical or nonsurgical treatment.
whyItMatters: Along with EMBOLISE, STEM strengthened the case for MMA embolization as an adjunct in selected symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma patients and helps explain later specialty-guideline adoption. ED clinicians should view this as a consultation and downstream-treatment development rather than a replacement for urgent decompression when clinically indicated.
evidenceNotes: NEJM publisher metadata verifies publication online on 2024-11-20 even though the print issue was 2025-02-27; PubMed verifies DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2409845 and PMID 39565980. The publisher abstract and PubMed abstract were reviewed; the full article was not reviewed end-to-end. Later society guidance adopted adjunctive MMA embolization for selected chronic subdural hematoma, but the total randomized evidence remains heterogeneous. No retraction was identified in the targeted cross-check.
primaryEndpoint: Composite treatment failure within 180 days: recurrent or residual chronic subdural hematoma greater than 10 mm, reoperation or surgical rescue, or major disabling stroke, myocardial infarction, or neurologic death.
